title: Micro-latency fallback profiles & SDK surface notes
content:
High-level intent:
This note is a lightweight PRD-sketch exploring a small set of primitives to deliver predictable sub-100ms perceived latency for interactive clients while preserving deterministic tool-calling and structured/typed incremental output. Focus: SDK ergonomics for low-memory/mobile clients, server-side fallback profiles (micro-latency vs cost), and deterministic handshake for tool calls so we can safely fall back across model variants/regions.

Context / problem we're solving (short):
- Many customers want near-instant perceived responses in chat-like flows (autocomplete, code edit hints, micro-UX) where tokens are short.
- Current streaming behavior optimizes for throughput and correctness but not perceived latency; clients often wait for a full chunk or a complete JSON object before rendering.
- Tool-calls (search, DB write, code-exec) are brittle under partial-streaming: if the hosted model stalls or we switch region/model the client and server must agree on whether the tool was invoked and the resulting side-effect.
- Mobile & embedded SDKs need tiny runtime memory and a simple surface (no heavy incremental JSON parsing).

Goal (product):
- Provide a 1–2 line SDK integration pattern that enables: progressive rendering with typed frames, deterministic idempotent tool-call handshake, and server-driven micro-latency fallback profiles that gracefully degrade to cheaper/laggier models while preserving consistency.
- Make it trivial for app developers to opt into an aggressive low-latency pipeline with clear tradeoffs and observable guardrails.

Non-goals:
- This doc does not design the entire server routing stack or pricing model. It assumes those pieces exist and will be annotated by infra and billing.
- Not covering on-prem private-deploy specifics (we'll have a separate operational guide).

Personas:
- Product engineer building an in-app autocomplete that wants near-immediate feedback but cares about correctness for tool-backed actions.
- Mobile SDK maintainer who must support <3MB binary overhead and a tiny runtime.
- Platform SRE who needs clear observability signals when the system falls back.

Success metrics (initial):
- 90th percentile perceived-first-byte latency for short-turn chat reduced by 30% on midsize customers after opt-in.
- Tool-call duplication incidents (where the same external action executed twice) remain <0.01% after fallback rollouts.
- Developer adoption: >10 customers on the micro-latency profile in the first quarter post-launch.

Key UX constraints and assumptions:
- Clients must accept partial typed frames (simple framing) and be able to render incremental text spans without parsing heavyweight JSON libraries.
- Tool-side effects must be guarded by a lightweight 2-phase commit-ish handshake controlled by the platform (idempotency token + opt-out for exactly-once expensive ops).
- When server routes to cheaper models, the partial output may be lower fidelity; SDKs must provide simple signals for clients to either continue, revalidate, or show a fallback UI.

Proposed primitives (high-level):
1) Progressive typed frame (ASCII-first, compact): each frame is newline-delimited, starts with a 1-2 letter type tag, then a compact payload. Minimal parsing on clients. Example stream (wire):

TEXT: Hello, wor
TEXT: ld!
TOOL: CALL;id=tok_42;name=search;scope=readonly
TOOL-RESP: id=tok_42;ok;hits=3
JSON-BLOCK: {"meta":...}
DONE

Notes: TEXT frames are renderable as they arrive. TOOL frames are control frames. JSON-BLOCK is base64-optional for big structured blobs.

2) Tool-call deterministic handshake (server-side policy + SDK surface):
- Client initiates a tool-call by including an explicit tool intent in the request metadata (tool_hint: name, idempotency_key) or by signaling that the model may call tools.
- Server assigns a platform-level call id (pcall_id) before dispatching to the model or target variant. The model emits a TOOL frame with that pcall_id when it wants a call executed.
- Execution semantics: the platform ensures at-most-once within a time window for idempotent ops using pcall_id + idempotency_key mapping and by default retries only when safe.
- If the request is routed to a fallback model that cannot produce a TOOL frame, the platform will synthesize a TOOLTENTATIVE frame indicating the intent, and the SDK can either:
   a) Defer execution until a committed TOOL frame arrives (blocking behaviour), or
   b) Execute tentatively if app configured accept_tentative_tool=true (UI must show a provisional state).

3) Micro-latency fallback profiles (server-side):
- Profiles are named bundles (e.g., "micro-latency", "balanced", "cost-efficient") that control routing priority, prefetching (predictive KV caching), and max model switch latency.
- Micro-latency profile rules: prefer local low-seq model shards, enable speculative prefetch for common completions, aggressively stream partial tokens as TEXT frames (no waiting for sentence boundaries), and allow speculative tool-call synthesis (TOOLTENTATIVE).
- Fallback policy: if primary variant fails to meet a tight RTT budget, route to fallback within 12–40ms (configurable). When routing happens, emit a ROUTE-FALLBACK frame with reason+score so SDKs can surface a subtle UI badge.

SDK ergonomics (thin-client pattern):
- Minimal runtime parse: SDK exposes an onFrame(callback) with frameType and payload string. Default handlers for TEXT and TOOL simplify integration. Example JS-ish surface:

const stream = redwood.stream(req)
stream.onFrame((type, payload) => {
  if (type === 'TEXT') render.append(payload)
  if (type === 'TOOL') toolDispatcher.run(payload)
  if (type === 'ROUTE-FALLBACK') telemetry.emit('fallback', payload)
})

- Lazy JSON: SDK provides helpers to rehydrate JSON-BLOCK frames on-demand (deferred base64 decode). Mobile can ignore JSON blocks until user expands.
- Resume tokens: All streams support a compact resume_token emitted every N frames. Clients reconnecting provide resume_token to continue stream without re-running model. Resume_token should be a platform opaque string.
- Backpressure: SDK exposes a small backpressure API: stream.shed(mode) where mode is 'drop-late-text'|'pause-tools' to enable degraded rendering when network is saturated.

Observability + telemetry requirements:
- New metrics: frames_per_second, avg_first_text_latency, tool-intent-rate, tool-exec-duplication-rate, fallback-routing-rate, fallback-reason-dist.
- Each ROUTE-FALLBACK and TOOLTENTATIVE must include trace context and pcall_id so we can correlate duplication incidents.
- Provide a daily audit report for tool-call duplicate incidents per customer.

Failure modes and mitigations:
- Duplicate tool execution due to race across regions: mitigate by platform-level dedupe keyed by pcall_id + idempotency_key and by ensuring tool-call acknowledgment protocol needs pcall_id confirmation.
- Client shows provisional state but final result differs: encourage apps to use accept_tentative_tool=false for destructive ops (DB writes, payments) and allow accept_tentative_tool=true for read-only or UI-only hints. Document strongly.
- Resume token mismatch leading to partial replays: make resume_token strong-hash of request + short window state; provide server-side sanity checks and bounded replay limits.

Developer flows and samples (notes):
- Quickstart: opt-in by passing profile='micro-latency' and a small flag stream_mode='frame-lite'. SDK then uses default frame handlers.
- Migration: existing non-streaming clients can receive a special RESP-LEGACY frame when they call the streaming endpoint; allow an 'upgrade' header to transition slowly.

Rollout plan (phased):
- Phase 0: internal alpha (Infra + Applied ML + SDK team). Validate frame encoding, resume tokens, and dedupe logic. (2–3 sprints)
- Phase 1: limited beta with 5 customers in mobile-first use cases. Monitor duplication and fallback rates; require opt-in. (1 month)
- Phase 2: broader opt-in with usage quotas; add console observability tile. (1–2 months)
- Phase 3: GA with clarified SLAs and pricing.

Open questions (needs engineering input):
- How large a resume_token is acceptable across mobile networks? (target < 512 bytes).
- Exact guarantees on tool dedupe window (30s? 2m?). Suggest default 30s with customer-configurable TTL.
- Can the routing layer synthesize tool-call results for fallbacks safely for read-only ops (e.g., cached search results)? Need policy here.

Next immediate action items (owners):
- Miguel: prototype frame-lite encoder + minimal JS SDK handler (spike, 5 days).
- Sophie: spec resume_token format + dedupe TTL proposal (INF-2345).
- Daniel: infra checklist for route-fallback trace propagation and metrics (GH#7012).
- Ravi: draft customer-facing checklist for "accept_tentative_tool" UX guidance and sample messages.

Notes to self / rough TODOs:
- Add small sequence diagram for TOOL lifecycle: client request -> platform pcall_id -> model TOOL frame -> platform execute -> TOOL-RESP -> final commit frame.
- Think about how this interacts with offline clients who want a summary rather than incremental text. Maybe a compact-summary frame type later.

Bottom line: this is a low-risk opt-in path that we can ship to developers who prioritize perceived latency at the cost of some controlled ambiguity for tool execution. By combining compact typed frames, resume tokens, and platform-level pcall_id dedupe, we can deliver a developer-friendly SDK that keeps costly duplication rare and observable.

References & links (working):
- INF-2345: resume token design (ticket)
- GH#7012: route tracing + fallback instrumentation
- Confluence: hosted-streaming PRD (working link above)

End of draft. Feedback welcome — especially from applied-ml and infra teams on performance tradeoffs.
